- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.77) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% relative to historical mean or recent peak.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤0.27) or shows sharp drops, model often underestimates; adjust upward by 2–5% to account for potential rebound.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 75% above recent mean), model frequently overcorrects downward; apply a “lag correction” — reduce forecast by 1–3% for next 3–5 periods.
- If sentiment is volatile or mixed (alternating 0.27–0.80), model tends to overfit short-term noise; smooth forecasts by averaging last 3–5 periods or applying a 10% dampening factor.
- In high-sentiment environments (e.g., 0.80+), model often fails to capture mean reversion; apply a “mean reversion bias” — subtract 1–3% of recent 10-day average from forecast if price is above 75% of 30-day moving average.
- For 30-day horizon, model consistently overestimates in early periods (first 5–7 days) when sentiment is rising; reduce first 5 forecasts by 3–7% to align with observed lagged behavior.
- If sentiment is consistently low (≤0.30) and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop; increase forecast by 1–3% to reflect potential “sudden drop” or “panic sell-off” bias.
